item.title: Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis Enables Scalable Modeling of Human and Machine Reasoning
item.description:
Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis Enables Scalable Modeling of Human and Machine Reasoning

Symbolic models offer a powerful account of cognition, but their scope has historically been limited by the need for hand‑engineering and computational tractability. A new study shows how advances in artificial intelligence can scale symbolic modeling and help overcome these engineering limitations.

🔍 Overview

The authors introduce Behavior‑Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS), an approach for automated search of interpretable, deterministic symbolic programs that verifiably reproduce behavior. BCSS is applied to model both human and machine behavior across hundreds of challenging reasoning problems.

🧩 How it works

  • BCSS automatically searches for symbolic programs that match observed behavior.
  • The resulting programs are deterministic and interpretable, allowing direct verification against the original behavior.
  • The method is employed on a large suite of reasoning tasks, covering both people and black‑box AI systems.

⚙️ Key details

  • Historical limitation: symbolic models required extensive hand‑engineering and faced computational tractability issues.
  • AI‑enabled scaling: modern AI techniques make it feasible to synthesize symbolic models at scale.
  • Empirical findings:
    • Both people and machines tend to oversimplify problem structure.
    • They often adopt partial rules that explain only part of their observations.
    • They misinfer dependencies between problem features.
  • Resource modulation: the identified signatures are affected by the resources available to the reasoner; higher reasoning effort predicts greater simplification and explanation by machines.
  • Satisficing link: the shared patterns resemble satisficing mechanisms in both humans and machines.
  • General utility: BCSS provides a framework for interpreting and comparing rule‑based reasoning across humans and black‑box AI systems.

🚀 Availability

  • ArXiv submission: 4 Nov 2026
  • Category: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  • Formats: PDF and HTML (experimental) are available on arXiv.

💡 Why it matters

  • Offers a path to overcome hand‑engineering bottlenecks in symbolic cognition modeling.
  • Provides interpretable, verifiable models for both human and AI reasoning.
  • Reveals common reasoning shortcuts shared by people and machines, informing future cognitive and AI research.
  • Establishes a general approach for comparing rule‑based reasoning across disparate systems.

#symbolicAI #interpretability #cognitiveModeling #AIresearch

Source: Synthesizing symbolic models of human and machine reasoning at scale Source: SAVeR$^2$: Reasoning-based Safety Alignment for Large Reasoning Models via Verifiable Rewards Source: CST-Bench: Benchmarking Counterfactual Spatial Transition Reasoning with Causal Transition On-Policy Self-Distillation Source: Enhancing Repository-Level Code Completion with Reinforcement Learning in Real-World Scenarios

item.title: Causal Study Reveals How Language Models Favor Certain Numbers
item.description:
Causal Study Reveals How Language Models Favor Certain Numbers

When a language model picks a number between 1 and 30, every integer is valid, yet the model can show a systematic preference. A new arXiv paper submitted on 4 Nov 2026 investigates where that preference originates and how it propagates through the model’s layers.

🔍 Overview

  • The study treats numerical choice as a controlled case for probing persistent state and conditional downstream processing in language models.
  • Experiments focus on a Qwen3‑4B model, examining how a small edit before the answer influences later token generation.

🧩 Methodology

  • Perturbation probing and gradient attribution are used to nominate individual neurons for activation interventions.
  • Interventions include:
    1. Cache and attention‑output replacements after a pre‑answer edit.
    2. Replacing the output of a single attention head versus replacing multiple heads jointly.
    3. Clamping later MLP outputs to values from the edited run.
  • Prompt tests separate influence from answer changes, using held‑out prompts and twelve fresh wordings.

⚙️ Key Findings

  • A pre‑answer edit that changes the intended answer from 17 to 15 still results in the model first emitting the token 1 in both edited and unedited runs.
  • After the edit, selective cache and attention‑output replacements trace part of the edit’s continuing influence on the second digit.
  • Replacing one attention head’s output or multiple heads jointly:
    • Restores the answer 17 immediately.
    • Produces different final log‑odds effects on the subsequent digits 7 versus 5.
  • Holding later MLP outputs at edited‑run values without any head replacement reduces the log‑odds effect gap from 0.119 nat to 0.0025 nat.
  • Later computation therefore changes how similar local contributions affect the continuation.
  • Retrospective estimates across eighteen contexts capture much of the probability movement but miss the selected answer switch.
  • Prompt tests show that a held‑out prompt can retain influence without switching the answer, and only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test; in that case, joint MLP clamping again narrows the gap while the answer stays 17.

💡 Why it matters

  • The results demonstrate that numerical preference can be traced to specific activation patterns and that persistent state can influence downstream token choices.
  • The paper emphasizes that these findings do not establish the origin or a complete circuit of natural numerical preference, highlighting the need for further work on interpretability and causal mechanisms in language models.

#numericalpreference #languagemodels #causalanalysis #interpretability

Source: When Every Choice Is Correct: A Causal Study of Numerical Preference in Language Models

item.title: New Research on Linguistic Representation and Script Commitment in LLMs
item.description:
New Research on Linguistic Representation and Script Commitment in LLMs

Recent research utilizing interpretability methods has provided new insights into how Large Language Models (LLMs) distribute script knowledge, localize linguistic selectivity, and encode morpho-syntactic information.

🔍 Overview

Researchers have investigated the distribution of script knowledge across LLM layers and the localization of linguistic selectivity using three distinct approaches:

  • Logistic regression probing and logit-lens analysis for script knowledge.
  • A probe-free framework using the Neuron Separability Index (NSI) for individual neuron selectivity.
  • Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs) to study the encoding of part-of-speech (PoS) categories.

🧩 How it works

Script Knowledge Distribution

Analysis of script knowledge reveals a two-stage process:

  • Early Layers: Both input and instructed output scripts are encoded here.
  • Intermediate Layers: Representations typically default to Latin.
  • Final Layers: Commitment to the actual output script emerges.

Linguistic Selectivity (NSI)

The Neuron Separability Index (NSI) quantifies how reliably single neurons differentiate grammatical from ungrammatical constructions without parameter updates. Findings include:

  • Raw separability for morphological and syntactic distinctions reaches near-peak levels earlier than for conceptual distinctions or the syntax-semantics interface.
  • Single-unit selectivity is sparse, weak, and narrowly tuned after permutation normalization.
  • “Grandmother neurons” that are strongly selective are rare.

Morpho-syntactic Encoding (SAEs)

Using part-of-speech (PoS) categories as a test case, researchers found:

  • PoS distinctions are highly recoverable from SAE activations but do not follow one-to-one latent/category mappings.
  • Information is localized in a distributed, category-dependent form rather than atomic grammatical features.
  • Categories are supported by compact groups of sparse latents that remain stable on held-out data.

💡 Why it matters

Evidence linking script commitment to model depth suggests implications for the design of inclusive multilingual architectures, particularly as smaller models exhibit weaker script-following performance.

#LLM #Interpretability #NLP #NeuralNetworks

Source: Script Choice in LLMs: Evidence for Late-Layer Commitment Source: Grammatical “grandmother neurons” are rare in LLMs Source: Parts-of-Speech as Emergent Categories in SAE Latent Space
